lines: A real interpreter runs one program with a real branch, and this run takes the branch whose every operation stays inside one fixed buffer.
Does the real checker, run only on this branch's own operations, find a violation?
answer: Every operation on this branch stays inside the buffer.

lines: Run it for real: the real checker, run over every operation this branch actually takes, finds no violation at all.
The identical interpreter now runs the branch its first run never took, which holds a real, genuinely out of bounds operation.
Does the checker catch it this time?
answer: Caught, the moment a run actually takes the branch that holds it.

lines: Run it for real: the real checker, run over this branch's own operations, genuinely catches the violation the instant this run actually reaches it.
steps.takeaway: The identical violation is real and checkable the instant a run actually reaches it.

lines: The safe branch's own run never took the other branch at all.
How many of the other branch's own operations did that first run's checker actually examine?
answer: That branch was never taken, so it was never checked.

lines: Run it for real: the safe branch run genuinely examined exactly its own operations and none of the other branch's; the violation sat there, real and uninspected, the whole time.
steps.takeaway: A checker that never runs a branch never asks it a single question.

lines: Two real, independent sources on the identical limitation agree, in their own words.
A checker can tell you whether one particular way of running your code causes undefined behavior in one particular execution, never every execution a program could ever take.
steps.takeaway: A run-based checker's silence means this run found nothing, not that nothing is there.

lines: So here's what this topic's own tiny interpreter is really standing in for: a real detection tool doesn't read your code and reason about every path it could ever take, it watches one actual execution and reports exactly what that one execution did.

That's a genuinely useful thing to watch, and it's also a genuinely narrower thing than people sometimes assume a clean run means: a clean run says this path was fine, it never says every path would have been.

And that closes out what this whole chapter has been building toward: a documented contract decided what a caller was even allowed to reach, a validity rule decided what counted as a legal value once they reached it.
And now a checker decides, one actual execution at a time, whether either rule was ever actually broken.
None of the three can do the other one's job, and together they're still only as good as the paths somebody actually bothered to run.
